title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Important experimental design facts are explicit: baseline and guarded conditions shared a single initial generation per task (shared‑initial design) and the guarded pipeline invoked repair only when the deterministic validator reported failure; provider_call_audit records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and total model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial calls + 1 repair call). Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially increases pass rate (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported. We interpret this as a ceiling effect combined with minimal GVR engagement (repair invoked once). We report full confirmatory accounting, discuss implications for benchmark design, and point readers to the sealed preregistration and archived execution artifacts for per‑task diagnostics and provider traces.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) have been proposed to assist network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior studies show LLMs can draft device configurations but often produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; combining generation with deterministic verifiers and localized repair can reduce such errors. The NetOps community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple operationally structured intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and that support sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (generate–validate–repair, GVR) versus single‑pass generation. To address this gap we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a guarded GVR pipeline produces a materially higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget. Our contributions are: (1) a sealed preregistered benchmark design and deterministic validator specification; (2) an autonomous, archived paired N=300 confirmatory comparison (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) using declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0); and (3) a complete archival bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts) to enable community reuse and extension. The final research question: Can a standardized synthetic task set and deterministic validator reveal a material per‑task correctness advantage for an automated GVR pipeline over a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget?
sections.related_work: Surveys and focused technical studies document strong interest in LLMs for NetOps and repeatedly flag evaluation, realism, and safety gaps; they also report that verifier‑assisted architectures improve final correctness in limited experiments. Work on intent→configuration translation and LLM‑assisted configuration synthesis demonstrates feasibility but often relies on human oversight or limited testbeds. Studies on GVR‑style and context‑aware iterative prompting report improved misconfiguration detection/correction in narrow datasets, and separate literature highlights prompt injection, jailbreaks, and hallucination as operational risks for LLM‑driven workflows. Collectively these works motivate a sealed, artifact‑grounded, machine‑checkable confirmatory comparison that (a) fixes generation variance via a shared‑initial design and (b) isolates repair efficacy under a constrained repair budget and deterministic validation semantics. We cite representative verified sources that synthesize these findings and gaps.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and confirmatory hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). Design and shared‑initial semantics. The study used a paired binary design with a single shared initial generation per task. That shared candidate was the baseline single‑pass result. For the guarded condition the pipeline ran the deterministic validator on the same shared candidate and, only if the validator reported failure, was allowed up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial design intentionally controls for generation variance: baseline and guarded initially receive identical text, so any guarded improvement must result from an invoked repair. Provider accounting shows stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, i.e., repair was invoked exactly once across N=300 tasks. Task bank and validator. The deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks evenly distributed across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, and workflow_policies (required sequence constraints). The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements the scoring rule “full_intent_constraint_validation” and returns score=1 with reason VALID_CONFIGURATION only when all declared constraints are satisfied. Model and adapter configuration. Declared model and runtime settings (execution/model_configuration.json) were: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. In our hosted adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) a deterministic sampling mode was used to ensure repeatable shared‑initial outputs across runs: ‘‘temperature = null’’ indicates that no stochastic temperature parameter was applied by the pipeline and that the hosted adapter invoked the provider in a deterministic sampling mode (the execution manifest and execution/provider_calls entries record the exact provider call and any provider‑exposed determinism tokens). Reproducers seeking bit‑for‑bit replication should use the execution/model_configuration.json plus the archived per‑call provider traces (execution/provider_calls/) as authoritative references for the provider conditions that produced the recorded outputs. Preregistered analysis plan. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The prescribed test was exact McNemar two‑sided with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Exclusion rules and missingness. Exclusions removed ambiguous specifications or contamination (none occurred). Missingness plan required ≥270 completed pairs for confirmatory inference; the run produced 300 complete pairs.
sections.results: Execution and accounting. The run completed per the preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 300. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation) records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; therefore the guarded repair stage executed exactly once under the preregistered repair budget. Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis artifacts) are: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Interpretation of contingency and p‑value. With discordant counts n10=1 and n01=0 the exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value equals 1.0 under the implemented test: the single discordant outcome is insufficient to reject the null of equal paired proportions given the small discordant sample and the two‑sided test's exact enumeration. Practically, the near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) leaves almost no room for the preregistered detectable paired effect (0.10). Discordant episode and repair accounting. The run's provider accounting shows a single repair invocation; the complete per‑episode record that contains the baseline failure, the guarded success, and the repair provider trace (provider request/response with timestamps) is archived verbatim in the execution bundle. The entire paired outcomes and all per‑task validator diagnostics are included in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and indexed in the full artifact manifest in the bundle; reproducer tools may extract the specific pair id and the repair provider trace SHA‑256 from that manifest. Representative per‑task examples. Six representative task scoring JSONs and their shared initial response texts are included in the archival bundle (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json, … task-000006-*.json) and show validator traces with score=1 for both baseline and guarded conditions in the examples presented here; none of those six examples invoked repair. Statistical power sensitivity. The preregistered power calculation targeted detectability of an absolute paired difference of 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. The observed baseline success rate 0.9967 invalidates that detectability assumption: with baseline near 1.0 the study is underpowered to detect a 0.10 paired improvement because the maximum achievable paired improvement is small. This ceiling explains the null confirmatory outcome.
sections.discussion: Null and ceiling‑effect diagnosis. Two factors explain the lack of a measurable GVR advantage on this benchmark: (1) ceiling effect — the baseline single‑pass generator already satisfied the deterministic validator on 299/300 tasks; and (2) minimal GVR engagement — the guarded repair stage executed once (repair stage_counts = 1). Because the guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline, the paired test primarily compared identical shared initial candidates rather than repaired alternatives. Practical implications for benchmark design. To reveal practical repair value, future benchmarks should (a) increase task difficulty or explicitly seed failing initial candidates, (b) permit larger or iterative repair budgets per task, (c) evaluate multiple independent generations per task (to widen generator variance), and/or (d) adopt stateful validators that model in‑flight dynamics and time‑ordered side effects rather than snapshot checks. These concrete adjustments follow directly from the logged provider accounting and per‑task validator diagnostics archived in the execution bundle. Deterministic sampling and reproducibility. The hosted adapter used a deterministic sampling mode so that shared‑initial outputs were reproducible under the same provider conditions. In practice “temperature = null” in execution/model_configuration.json indicates that the pipeline did not apply stochastic temperature sampling; the hosted adapter invoked the provider under deterministic emission settings and recorded provider‑reported metadata per call. Exact bit‑for‑bit reproduction therefore requires (a) the same provider release and deterministic invocation semantics, and (b) use of the archived provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/) combined with execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and the raw_results.jsonl index (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Limits on external validity. Tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and the deterministic validator enforces snapshot intent constraints without modeling vendor execution idiosyncrasies or runtime side effects. The study evaluated a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a single fixed repair budget and therefore does not establish multi‑model or production generality. Failure‑mode analysis limits. Only one discordant pair (n10=1) was observed, which leaves exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive; the per‑task diagnostics are archived for future meta‑analysis by the community.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Crucially, the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about the general effectiveness of automatic repair. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can extend this benchmark with harder tasks, stateful validators, larger repair budgets, and multi‑model comparisons to better evaluate when GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or runtime side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture full production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact artifact files that contain (a) the single repair provider trace and its SHA‑256 and (b) the identifier and full validator diagnostic excerpt for the single baseline failure episode are present in the archived execution bundle (execution/provider_calls/, execution/scoring/, execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and are authoritative; the execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and the full artifact hash manifest index those per‑item records for retrieval.
